newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. economist sees Fed rate hike by mid-year.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economist sees Fed rate hike by mid-year.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve will likely raise interest rates moderately by mid-year to quell incipient inflation, a U.S. economist said Friday.

"I would say that there is a 50/50 chance that the Fed will raise rates at its May 20 meeting and I'm certainly looking for one or maybe two quarter-point tightenings by the summer," said David Jones, vice chairman and chief economist of Aubrey G. Lanston & Co.
Jones was speaking at a forum sponsored by IBJ Asia in Hong Kong.
He said key U.S. labour market indicators -- the number of people working, hours worked, the unemployment rate and hourly earnings -- are showing early signs of labour market tightness.
"Red signals are flashing but there is not enough strain yet for the Fed to tighten aggressively," said Jones.
He said the story is the same in the product market, where there are signs of inflationary pressures, but these are not significant enough to encourage Fed action right now.
But Jones said excess global liquidity will lead to asset inflation in the United States in the first half of this year.
"It is inevitable that liquidity will spill over into real assets," he said.

A Fed move to increase the federal funds rate to 5.50 or 5.75 percent by mid-year from 5.25 percent now is likely to slow the economy enough that it would settle back into its trend of steady growth and low inflation, he said.

Jones forecast a year-end U.S. growth rate of about 2.6 percent on a fourth quarter 1997 versus fourth quarter 1996 basis, which he said was slightly above the long-term equilibrium rate of 2.3 percent.
He said he saw inflation mostly steady at 3.25-3.5 percent in 1997 but rising to four percent in 1998.
The U.S. dollar could rise to 130 yen this year from the 122.90 level now, Jones said.
He said the dollar could reach 180 German marks versus Friday's 1.6855, aided by relative growth differentials.

Speaking at the same forum, Adolf Rosenstock, senior economist at IBJ Frankfurt, said the outlook for Europe is bright, but that Germany may have trouble fulfilling deficit criteria for European Monetary Union in coming months.
"In light of recent data," said Rosenstock, "you have to doubt that (Germany's) recovery will come soon enough to meet the EMU criteria."
